mcq.q: Which query is BM25 likely to handle better than dense retrieval?
options: "how do I feel valued at work"
mcq.why: Exact identifiers and codes favour lexical matching.

mcq.q: What is an inverted index?
options: A reversed copy of each document
A list of documents sorted by length
A map from each term to the list of documents containing it
mcq.why: Finding “refund” means reading one posting list.

mcq.q: How do TF-IDF and BM25 score a document?
options: By how often query terms occur in it, weighted by how rare each term is in the collection
mcq.why: Rare terms carry more weight than common ones.
distractors: Length is a correction, not the score.

mcq.q: What does BM25's saturation parameter k₁ do?
options: Makes extra occurrences of a term add less and less
mcq.why: The tenth occurrence adds little.

mcq.q: What does BM25's parameter b do?
options: Normalises for document length, so long documents are not favoured just for being long
mcq.why: Typically b ≈ 0.75.

mcq.q: With N = 8 documents and a term in 1 of them, what is IDF = ln(1 + (N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5))?
BM25 finds nothing for “can't log in” because the documents say “login” and “sign in”. What is this called, and what helps?
mcq.why: Dense retrieval matches meaning across different words.

mcq.q: What is learned sparse retrieval (for example SPLADE)?
options: A model assigns weights to vocabulary terms, including related ones, stored in an inverted index
mcq.why: It combines keyword-index efficiency with some semantic matching.

mcq.q: A team assumes their vector database chose a good embedding model. What is wrong?
options: Embedding models are all the same
A vector database only stores and searches vectors; choosing and evaluating the model is your job
mcq.why: Evaluate embedding models on your queries.

mcq.q: Why does BM25 need no training?
options: It uses term statistics from the corpus itself
It is pretrained by its vendor
mcq.why: Counts and document frequencies are all it needs.

interview.q: Explain how BM25 scores a document.
Compare keyword search and dense retrieval.
covers: No training versus an embedding model

interview.q: What is an inverted index, and why is it fast?
Users search for error codes and paraphrased problems. How do you design retrieval?
interview.followUp: How would you weight the two legs?

interview.q: Your dense retriever misses exact product codes. What do you do?
{company}'s customers paste transaction references and write Hinglish complaints. Design retrieval for both.
Design retrieval for a corpus mixing short product listings and long policy documents.
When would you consider learned sparse retrieval?
covers: Need keyword efficiency plus semantic matching
Evaluate against hybrid BM25 plus dense

mcq.q: Why use reciprocal rank fusion?
options: It needs no normalisation of different score scales
It is the most accurate reranker
mcq.why: RRF uses ranks only, so BM25 and cosine scores need not share a scale.

mcq.q: Where must permission filtering happen?
options: In retrieval, before content reaches the model
mcq.why: Once the model has seen restricted text, the leak has already happened.

mcq.q: With RRF (k = 60), a document ranked 1st by BM25 and 3rd by dense search scores what?
distractors: That counts only the BM25 rank.

mcq.q: What does a cross-encoder reranker do?
options: Reads query and passage together and scores relevance, re-scoring the top 50–200 candidates
mcq.why: Much more accurate than separate embeddings, but too slow for the whole corpus.

mcq.q: What is the difference between pre-filtering and post-filtering?
options: Pre-filtering is done by the user
Pre-filtering applies the filter during search; post-filtering removes results afterwards
mcq.why: Selective post-filters can leave too few results.
distractors: They differ in when the filter applies.

mcq.q: A highly selective filter is applied after retrieving the top 20. What can happen?
mcq.why: Apply selective filters inside the search.

mcq.q: Which steps belong to context assembly?
options: Deduplicate, merge adjacent chunks, order, label with citation IDs, fit the token budget
mcq.why: Assembly prepares what the model sees (7.3).

mcq.q: A team adds raw BM25 scores to cosine similarities to rank results. What is wrong?
options: The scores have different scales and meanings; fuse by rank (RRF) or normalise carefully
mcq.why: RRF needs no score normalisation because it uses ranks.

mcq.q: What is a typical latency budget for filters plus retrieval, and for reranking on GPU?
mcq.why: Reranking is slower on CPU.

mcq.q: In RRF, what does a small k do?
options: Emphasises the top ranks more strongly
mcq.why: Large k flattens differences.

interview.q: Explain hybrid retrieval and reciprocal rank fusion.
Why rerank, and where does a reranker sit?
covers: Too slow for the whole corpus

interview.q: Why must permission filters be applied inside retrieval?
covers: Post-filtering can leak or starve results

interview.q: Design a production retrieval pipeline with a latency budget.
Selective filters leave users with too few results. How do you fix it?
{company} needs in-stock, deliverable products in search results. Design the filtering and ranking.
covers: Stock and pincode filters inside search

interview.q: Design context assembly for a RAG system with strict token budgets.
How would you decide whether a reranker is worth its latency?

mcq.q: What kind of problem does RAG solve, and what kind does fine-tuning solve?
options: RAG: a knowledge problem; fine-tuning: a behaviour problem
RAG: a behaviour problem; fine-tuning: a knowledge problem
mcq.why: RAG supplies missing facts with sources; fine-tuning changes format, style or decision patterns.

mcq.q: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to inject facts?
options: Expensive to update, hard to delete, no citations, and recall of tuned facts is unreliable
mcq.why: Facts belong in retrievable, citable, deletable sources.
distractors: Cost is one of its problems.
Format is what it does well.

mcq.q: Policies change every week and answers must cite them. Which approach fits?
mcq.why: Re-index on change and cite policy IDs.
distractors: Does not scale to thousands of policies.

mcq.q: Answers are correct but not in the mandated format, and few-shot prompting costs too many tokens. What fits?
options: A small fine-tune for the format, keeping RAG for facts
mcq.why: A behaviour gap that prompting cannot close cheaply.
distractors: Size may not fix format cheaply.

mcq.q: What should you always start with?
options: Prompting plus RAG, fine-tuning only when evaluation shows a behaviour gap
mcq.why: Fine-tune when evidence says prompting cannot close the gap (13.1).

mcq.q: A fact was fine-tuned into a model, and the source document has now been deleted. What happens to the fact?
options: The model asks for the document
It may remain in the weights
The model refuses to mention it
mcq.why: Deleting the source does not remove what the weights learned.

mcq.q: Users need answers traceable to sources. Which approach provides that?
mcq.why: Retrieved chunks carry IDs to cite.

mcq.q: The model lacks long-tail facts about your niche products. What helps most?
options: Retrieval of those facts at question time
mcq.why: Long-tail facts are a knowledge gap.

mcq.q: Which statement describes using both approaches together?
options: RAG supplies the facts; a fine-tune shapes the format or behaviour
Fine-tuning supplies facts; RAG supplies format
Using both removes the need for evaluation
mcq.why: The bank example in the topic does exactly this.

mcq.q: Why might a team fine-tune for format instead of using few-shot examples?
options: Few-shot examples cost too many tokens on every call
mcq.why: Repeated examples add cost and latency to every request.

interview.q: When would you use RAG, fine-tuning, or both?
covers: Both when facts and format both matter

interview.q: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add facts?
What does “traceable to sources” require in a RAG system?
A stakeholder wants to fine-tune the model on the company wiki. How do you respond?
covers: Wiki facts change and have permissions
Fine-tune only for measured behaviour gaps
interview.followUp: What evidence would justify the fine-tune?

interview.q: Your RAG assistant is accurate but ignores the required answer format. What do you try, in order?
{company}'s catalogue changes daily. Design how {assistant} gets product facts and how its reply style is tuned.
covers: Retrieval and tools for listings, prices, stock
Small fine-tune or prompt for style

interview.q: Design an assistant over 3,000 internal policies that change weekly, with role-based access.
covers: Format via prompt or small fine-tune

interview.q: How do you handle a user's request to delete their data when a model may have been trained on it?
covers: Prefer retrieval so data can be deleted at the source
Track what data went into each fine-tune
Retrain or retire models if needed

mcq.q: Which RAG stages run offline, and which online?
options: Ingest, parse, clean, chunk, embed and index offline; retrieve and generate per question
mcq.why: Offline stages run continuously at scale (chapter 10).
distractors: Preparing documents per question would be too slow.

mcq.q: Which stage caps the quality of everything downstream?
mcq.why: Text lost or garbled in parsing cannot be retrieved later (10.3).
distractors: Generation depends on what retrieval provides.

mcq.q: What is a typical chunk size, and how should chunks be split?
options: About 200–800 tokens, split on headings and paragraphs with small overlaps
mcq.why: Small enough to be specific, large enough to be self-contained.

mcq.q: Why prepend a header such as the document title and section path to each chunk?
options: So the chunk makes sense on its own for embedding, retrieval and citation
mcq.why: “The limit is 5 days per year” becomes unambiguous with its section path.

mcq.q: What does chunk overlap do?
options: Protects sentences that straddle a boundary, at the cost of extra storage
mcq.why: Overlapping text appears in two chunks.

mcq.q: Why record the embedding model's name and version with each vector?
options: Changing the model requires re-embedding everything (10.7)
mcq.why: Vectors from different models are not comparable.

mcq.q: What does the index store?
options: Vectors in an ANN index, text in a keyword index, and metadata for filtering
mcq.why: Hybrid search and permission filters need all three.
distractors: Keyword search and filters need more.

mcq.q: Fixed-size chunks cut a rule away from its exception. What fixes it?
options: Paragraph- or structure-aware chunking that keeps sections intact
mcq.why: The chunking figure shows this directly.
distractors: The model never sees the exception.

mcq.q: PDF parsing is poor and answers are wrong. A team switches to a stronger answer model. What is likely?
mcq.why: The model cannot use text that parsing lost.
distractors: The model still lacks correct text.

mcq.q: 10,000 documents average 3,000 tokens each. With 500-token chunks and no overlap, about how many chunks is that?
mcq.why: 6 chunks per document × 10,000 documents.

interview.q: Walk through the RAG pipeline end to end.
covers: Retrieve, filter, rerank, generate with citations

interview.q: How do you choose a chunking strategy?
Why does parsing quality matter so much?
Your answers miss exceptions that are in the documents. Where do you look?
covers: Chunk boundaries splitting rules from exceptions
interview.followUp: How would you build a test that catches this?

interview.q: What metadata would you store with each chunk, and why?
{company}'s fare rules keep a fee and its exception in separate sentences. Design the chunking.
covers: Fee and exception in the same chunk
Header with product and fare family

interview.q: Design an ingestion pipeline for 50,000 mixed-format documents.
How would you evaluate the effect of chunk size on answer quality?

mcq.q: Brute-force search over 10 million 768-dimension vectors takes about how many multiply-adds per query?
distractors: Three orders of magnitude too low.

mcq.q: What do approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes trade?
options: A little recall for orders-of-magnitude speed
mcq.why: Exact search is fine for thousands of vectors, too slow for millions at high query rates.
distractors: They mainly trade recall for speed.

mcq.q: How does HNSW search work?
options: Start at a sparse top layer, greedily move closer to the query, drop a layer, and repeat
Cluster vectors and search one cluster
mcq.why: Upper layers act as express lanes with long links.

mcq.q: Which HNSW parameter controls the recall–latency trade-off at query time?
mcq.why: More candidates explored means higher recall and more latency.
distractors: M sets links per node (memory and recall).

mcq.q: How does an IVF index search?
options: Cluster vectors with k-means and search only the nprobe nearest clusters
mcq.why: More probes raise recall and cost.

mcq.q: How much memory do 10 million 768-dimension float32 vectors need?
mcq.why: 10⁷ × 768 × 4 bytes ≈ 30.7 GB, before index overhead.

mcq.q: With int8 scalar quantisation instead of float32, how large are those vectors?
mcq.why: 4× smaller than float32. Binary would be about 0.96 GB (32× smaller).

mcq.q: What is the common pattern for searching quantised vectors?
options: Search the compressed vectors, then re-score the top candidates with full-precision vectors
mcq.why: Re-scoring recovers most of the lost recall.

mcq.q: efSearch 40 gives Recall@10 0.91 at 2 ms; efSearch 200 gives 0.985 at 7 ms. How should you choose?
options: By how much a missed chunk costs versus the latency budget, measured on your own data
mcq.why: The right point depends on the application.
distractors: Too many misses may be unacceptable.

mcq.q: Retrieved passages are the wrong ones, though ANN recall against exact search is 0.99. What will raising ANN recall do?
options: Little: the representation ranks the wrong passages close; fix the embeddings or retrieval method
mcq.why: ANN recall measures agreement with exact search, not relevance.
distractors: Exact search would return the same wrong passages.
It would slightly improve agreement, not relevance.

interview.q: Why do vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour search?
covers: Brute force cost grows with corpus size
ANN trades a little recall for speed
Fine to use exact search for small corpora

interview.q: Explain how HNSW works and what M, efConstruction and efSearch control.
What are scalar, product and binary quantisation?
Size the memory for 50 million 768-dimension vectors and choose a quantisation strategy.
interview.followUp: Where would you keep the full-precision vectors?

interview.q: How do you tune efSearch for a production index?
{company} must search millions of listing vectors at festival peak. Design the index.
Explain the difference between ANN recall and retrieval quality.
covers: ANN recall: agreement with exact search

interview.q: When would you choose a disk-based index such as DiskANN?

mcq.q: What does query rewriting do?
options: Turns short or conversational questions into standalone search queries using history
mcq.why: “What about for contractors?” needs the earlier context.

mcq.q: What is HyDE?
options: Generating a hypothetical answer and embedding that instead of the question
mcq.why: The hypothetical answer may sit closer to relevant passages in embedding space.

mcq.q: What is decomposition?
options: Splitting a compound question into sub-queries, retrieving for each, then synthesising
mcq.why: For example, comparing policies in two countries.

mcq.q: What is multi-hop retrieval?
options: A chain of searches where each uses a fact found by the previous one
mcq.why: It is an iterative loop, effectively a small agent.

mcq.q: What keeps multi-hop retrieval from searching endlessly?
options: A hop limit and an abstain path
mcq.why: For example, at most 3 hops, then abstain.

mcq.q: How should citations be verified?
options: Check they are formatted as links
In code: each cited label exists, and the cited chunk supports the sentence (judge or overlap)
mcq.why: Then render citations as links to the source.

mcq.q: Retrieval scores are low and nothing supports an answer. What should the assistant do?
options: Abstain, say it was not found and offer a next step
mcq.why: A confident wrong answer is worse than an honest “not found”.
distractors: Unbounded retries cost time and money.

mcq.q: A user asks “what about for contractors?” after a question about leave. What must happen before retrieval?
options: Rewrite it into a standalone query, for example “parental leave policy for contractors”
mcq.why: The follow-up alone is ambiguous.

mcq.q: An answer cites a whole 80-page document. What is the problem?
options: The citation does not point to the clause the answer depends on
mcq.why: Cite the specific chunk.

mcq.q: When should you add multi-hop retrieval?
options: When evaluation shows single-shot retrieval fails on such questions
mcq.why: Each hop adds latency and a chance of error.

interview.q: Explain query rewriting, decomposition and multi-hop retrieval.
How do you make citations trustworthy?
When should a RAG assistant abstain?
Design citation verification for a RAG answer.
covers: Cited IDs exist among retrieved chunks
interview.followUp: What would you do with an answer that is right but cites the wrong chunk?

interview.q: Users ask follow-up questions that retrieve poorly. What do you change?
Questions about {company} bookings need both the booking and a rule. Design the multi-hop flow.
Design abstention behaviour that is honest but not unhelpful.
How would you evaluate a multi-hop retrieval system?

mcq.q: What are relevance labels (qrels)?
options: For each test query, which items are relevant, binary or graded
mcq.why: Every retrieval metric depends on them.

mcq.q: Why is Recall@k the key RAG metric?
options: It is the easiest to compute
If the answer chunk is not retrieved, the model cannot use it
mcq.why: Missing evidence caps answer quality.

mcq.q: A query has 3 relevant chunks; the top 5 results contain 2 of them. What is Recall@5?
For the same results (2 relevant in the top 5), what is Precision@5?
Over three queries, the first relevant result appears at ranks 2, 1 and 4. What is MRR?
Relevance grades at ranks 1–3 are [3, 0, 2]. What is DCG@3 with linear gains (gain = rel, divided by log₂(i + 1))?
distractors: That ignores the discount at rank 3.

mcq.q: What does the exponential gain (2^rel − 1) do compared with the linear gain?
options: Rewards the most relevant items far more
mcq.why: Always state which convention you report.
distractors: nDCG is normalised to at most 1.

mcq.q: A new retriever finds relevant passages that were never labelled. How do its metrics look?
options: Worse than they should: unlabelled relevant results count as misses
mcq.why: Pool results from several retrievers before labelling.

mcq.q: Retrieval metrics improved. Does that prove answers are better supported?
options: No: retrieval metrics do not measure whether the answer used the evidence
mcq.why: Evaluate answers separately (8.5).

mcq.q: What does an nDCG of 1.0 mean?
options: The ranking matches the ideal ordering
mcq.why: DCG is divided by the ideal DCG.

interview.q: Explain Recall@k, Precision@k, MRR and nDCG, and when each matters.
covers: Precision: share of the top k relevant

interview.q: Why is Recall@k the most important RAG retrieval metric?
covers: Choose k from the context budget

interview.q: How do incomplete labels bias retrieval comparisons?
covers: Unlabelled relevant results count as misses

interview.q: Build a retrieval benchmark from 200 real questions.
covers: Pool top results from several retrievers
Compute metrics with a tool such as ranx
interview.followUp: How would you keep the labels current as documents change?

interview.q: A new retriever has lower nDCG but users like it. What might be happening?
{company} reads only the first cited clause. Which retrieval metric would you report, and why?
covers: Tie metrics to how evidence is used

interview.q: Design retrieval reporting for a release review.
covers: Recall@k on a pooled labelled set

interview.q: How would you choose k for Recall@k in your reports?
covers: Match the number of chunks that reach the model
Report a small k for ranking quality
